props.text: You open Godot's particle system and find seven hundred checkboxes. You start clicking and hoping.

beats.narration_text: Particle. One short-lived simulation point — it has a position, a velocity, and an age, and when its age exceeds its lifetime, it's gone. Emitter. The source that spawns particles — it decides where and when new ones are born. Lifetime. How long a single particle lives, measured in seconds. Velocity. Rate of position change — direction and speed together. Emission cycle. One complete pass through the emitter's particle budget — its length equals the particle lifetime.

lecture.about: 5 prerequisite terms

shot.visual_intent: 5 prerequisite terms
shot.motion_claim: Terms arrive in spoken order

terms.meaning: One short-lived simulation point with position, velocity, and age
Source that spawns particles — controls when and where
How long a single particle lives (seconds)
Rate of position change — direction and speed
One pass through the particle budget; length = lifetime

beats.narration_text: One Moving Element.

lecture.about: Act I title

shot.visual_intent: Act I title
shot.motion_claim: Title card holds

beats.narration_text: In 1983, William Reeves described what he called fuzzy objects — fire and smoke in the Genesis sequence from Star Trek Two. His idea: an effect is a cloud of points that are born, that move and change, and that die. Every game engine you'll ever use runs exactly that loop.

lecture.about: Reeves 1983 — the loop named

shot.visual_intent: Reeves 1983 — the loop named
shot.motion_claim: Birth–life–death loop labels arrive in sequence; credit line fades in

show.event: Birth–life–death loop labels arrive in sequence; credit line fades in

beats.narration_text: Start with one dot. It has a position — where it is. It has a velocity — how fast it's moving and in which direction. It can have acceleration — what's changing the velocity. These are three different jobs, and they each play a role in how the dot moves.

lecture.about: Position / velocity / acceleration — three distinct roles

shot.visual_intent: Position / velocity / acceleration — three distinct roles
shot.motion_claim: Each arrow grows on its spoken cue; label lands on the word

show.event: Each arrow grows on its spoken cue; label lands on the word

beats.narration_text: Each frame, the velocity changes the position. Acceleration changes the velocity. In Godot, we multiply by delta — the time since the last frame — so the motion is the same speed on a slow machine and a fast one. One step. Done each frame.

lecture.about: Update equation: pos += vel × delta

shot.visual_intent: Update equation: pos += vel × delta
shot.motion_claim: Equation appears; dot steps forward frame by frame under it

show.event: Equation appears; dot steps forward frame by frame under it

beats.narration_text: Here's a dot starting at the bottom. Its velocity points up and slightly right. Each frame, delta time advances it. When gravity acts as acceleration pointing down, the dot curves. We're not drawing smoke yet. We're understanding the piece that smoke is made of.

lecture.about: One dot tracing a parabolic arc under gravity

shot.visual_intent: One dot tracing a parabolic arc under gravity
shot.motion_claim: Dot traces arc; velocity/position labels track; grid provides reference scale

show.event: Dot traces arc; velocity/position labels track; grid provides reference scale

beats.narration_text: Birth, Life and Removal.

lecture.about: Act II title

shot.visual_intent: Act II title
shot.motion_claim: Title card holds

beats.narration_text: Now give the dot an age. It starts at zero. Each frame, age increases by delta. When age exceeds lifetime — say one second — the dot is removed. While it lives, its opacity can track its normalized age: young and opaque, old and fading.

lecture.about: Age bar fills; opacity fades with normalized age

shot.visual_intent: Age bar fills; opacity fades with normalized age
shot.motion_claim: Age bar advances; dot opacity decreases proportionally; dot vanishes at lifetime

show.event: Age bar advances; dot opacity decreases proportionally; dot vanishes at lifetime

beats.narration_text: Spawn several. Each has its own age and velocity, with a little random variation. Now you have a small shower of points — born, traveling, fading, gone. This already looks like something: a brief burst, or a faint rain.

lecture.about: Small collection of dots — each with independent velocity and age

shot.visual_intent: Small collection of dots — each with independent velocity and age
shot.motion_claim: Dots spawn from emitter, fan outward with varied velocities, fade and vanish

show.event: Dots spawn from emitter, fan outward with varied velocities, fade and vanish

beats.narration_text: At twenty births per second with a two-second lifetime, after warm-up you tend toward about forty particles alive at once. That's an illustrative prediction — change either number and predict the new population. This is the planning tool. It's not a benchmark.

lecture.about: Population steady-state: 20/s × 2s ≈ 40 alive

shot.visual_intent: Population steady-state: 20/s × 2s ≈ 40 alive
shot.motion_claim: Formula builds; counter advances to 40; bar fills; 'not a benchmark' note fades in

show.event: Formula builds; counter advances to 40; bar fills; 'not a benchmark' note fades in

beats.narration_text: Remove the cleanup step. Every dot born stays forever. The count climbs without bound. The simulation bogs down. Returning cleanup lets the population settle. This is not a bug we're fixing — it's the lesson: a continuous effect stays alive while its individual particles expire. Cleanup is load-bearing.

lecture.about: Without removal, population climbs unbounded; with cleanup, it settles

shot.visual_intent: Without removal, population climbs unbounded; with cleanup, it settles
shot.motion_claim: Counter climbs past 120 with warning; then cleanup restores and counter falls to 40

show.event: Counter climbs past 120 with warning; then cleanup restores and counter falls to 40

beats.narration_text: One Emitter, Many Variations.

lecture.about: Act III title

shot.visual_intent: Act III title
shot.motion_claim: Title card holds

beats.narration_text: Move the emitter. The particles still carry their original velocity — they don't follow the source. They were born there, and they go where their velocity sends them.

lecture.about: Emitter moves; particles retain birth velocity (local_coords = false)

shot.visual_intent: Emitter moves; particles retain birth velocity (local_coords = false)
shot.motion_claim: Emitter dot moves left-to-right; particle trails diverge from birth positions

show.event: Emitter dot moves left-to-right; particle trails diverge from birth positions

beats.narration_text: Control the spread. A tight angle makes a jet. A wide spread makes a burst. Add random variation to the initial speed and the dot size. Now a handful of rules produces a cloud that looks organic. The key word is controlled: randomize everything and you lose the readable intention.

lecture.about: Narrow cone vs wide spread — same emitter, different angle ranges

shot.visual_intent: Narrow cone vs wide spread — same emitter, different angle ranges
shot.motion_claim: Left: tight jets; right: full-sphere burst; angles labeled

show.event: Left: tight jets; right: full-sphere burst; angles labeled

beats.narration_text: A shared force — say, wind — affects every particle. All the dots bend in the same direction. This is how gravity works too: one rule applied to every particle, every frame. The force is part of the process, not the emission.

lecture.about: Shared wind force bends all particles together

shot.visual_intent: Shared wind force bends all particles together
shot.motion_claim: Force vector arrow appears; all particles curve in wind direction

show.event: Force vector arrow appears; all particles curve in wind direction

beats.narration_text: Two modes. Spread births evenly across the lifetime and you get a continuous stream. Emit all of them at once — an explosiveness of one — and you get an instantaneous burst. Same parameters, different birth timing. That single knob is the difference between smoke and an explosion.

lecture.about: explosiveness 0 → stream vs explosiveness 1 → burst

shot.visual_intent: explosiveness 0 → stream vs explosiveness 1 → burst
shot.motion_claim: Left side: particles drip continuously; right side: all fire at once

show.event: Left side: particles drip continuously; right side: all fire at once

beats.narration_text: From Rules to Godot's Nodes.

lecture.about: Act IV title

shot.visual_intent: Act IV title
shot.motion_claim: Title card holds

beats.narration_text: Godot formalizes the loop into three parts. Emission: how many particles are born, when, and where — set on the particle node itself. Process: how each particle moves and changes over its life — set on a material or shader. Draw: what each particle looks like — a texture, a mesh, and a material on top of that. An effect can be wrong in any one part independently.

lecture.about: Emission / Process / Draw — three separable parts

shot.visual_intent: Emission / Process / Draw — three separable parts
shot.motion_claim: Table rows animate in on spoken cues; each row names Godot properties

show.event: Table rows animate in on spoken cues; each row names Godot properties

beats.narration_text: Godot gives you four nodes: G P U Particles 2D and 3D, and C P U Particles 2D and 3D. G P U nodes hand simulation to the graphics card and support sub-emitters, trails, and particle shaders. C P U nodes work on more hardware and are fully readable headlessly. The key difference is where the loop runs — not what the loop does.

lecture.about: Four node types — GPU vs CPU feature differences

shot.visual_intent: Four node types — GPU vs CPU feature differences
shot.motion_claim: Node names appear; feature rows highlight GPU-only features

show.event: Node names appear; feature rows highlight GPU-only features

props.title: Godot particle nodes — feature comparison (editor reconstruction)
props.code:
# Godot particle nodes — feature comparison
# Source: Chapter 9 "Four node types, two families"
GPUParticles2D / GPUParticles3D:
  process_material (ParticleProcessMaterial): YES
  sub_emitter: YES
  trail_enabled: YES
  amount_ratio: YES

CPUParticles2D / CPUParticles3D:
  process_material (ParticleProcessMaterial): NO (node props)
  sub_emitter: NO
  trail_enabled: NO
  near-feature parity, wider hardware support

beats.narration_text: The four timing properties. Lifetime: how long each particle lives — also the length of one emission cycle. Amount: how many particles in one cycle. Explosiveness: zero spreads births across the cycle; one fires them all at once. One shot: if true, the cycle runs exactly once. These four together determine when and how many particles appear.

lecture.about: amount / lifetime / explosiveness / one_shot — the four timing knobs

shot.visual_intent: amount / lifetime / explosiveness / one_shot — the four timing knobs
shot.motion_claim: Each property highlights on its spoken cue

show.event: Each property highlights on its spoken cue

props.code:
# GPUParticles2D — Inspector (Godot editor reconstruction)
# Source: Chapter 9 / Godot 4.7.2 class reference
amount = 10
lifetime = 1.0
explosiveness = 0.0
one_shot = false
preprocess = 0.0
randomness = 0.0
speed_scale = 1.0
fixed_fps = 30
emitting = true

beats.narration_text: The process material is shared between 2D and 3D nodes. Its defaults are three-dimensional: gravity pointing down on the Y axis in 3D, spread that fans into all three axes. In a 2D game, particles without Disable Z set will spray into an axis the camera never shows. Always enable Disable Z for 2D effects. The official demo README says exactly this.

lecture.about: Process material 3D defaults; Disable Z required for 2D

beats.narration_text: A particle node inherits its parent's transform and visibility. If the emitter's parent hides at the moment the effect should fire — a player dying, a pickup collected — the burst can be emitting and invisible. Parenting is a design choice, not a default. Choose the parent so the effect is still visible when it needs to be seen.

lecture.about: Parenting trap: parent hides → child hidden even while emitting

shot.visual_intent: Parenting trap: parent hides → child hidden even while emitting

show.event: Scene tree shows Player parent fading; burst node dims; then Main parent shown as correct choice

beats.narration_text: Replace the teaching simulation with a built-in node. Add G P U Particles 2D to a scene. Attach a Particle Process Material. Set the spread and velocity range. The node runs the same loop we built by hand — born, moved by the material's rules, drawn by its texture — but the engine handles the simulation. The artist still chooses the behavior.

lecture.about: Built-in particle node replacing hand-built loop — same rules, engine manages simulation

shot.visual_intent: Built-in particle node replacing hand-built loop — same rules, engine manages simulation
shot.motion_claim: Inspector values appear; correspondence to the hand-built loop is made explicit

show.event: Inspector values appear; correspondence to the hand-built loop is made explicit

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. For C S Y E seventy-two seventy, Building Virtual Environments. A particle system is a birth-life-death loop running on each short-lived element. Position, velocity, and acceleration are three distinct jobs the update step handles every frame. Removal is load-bearing: without it, the population climbs without bound. Three settings — amount, lifetime, and explosiveness — determine how many particles appear and when. Godot separates emission, process, and draw: each part can be wrong on its own.

lecture.about: Recap — six statements, two per page

shot.visual_intent: Recap — six statements, two per page
